title: Crash-safe two-slot recovery anchor installer
description: Objective: implement the media-loss install protocol that selects only a fully verified quiesced database generation. Deliverable: a @moe/store two-slot RecoveryAnchor installer with `PREPARED`/`INSTALLED` metadata outside restored payloads, inactive-slot database installation, one SQLite recovery transaction, database/artifact persistence and read-back verification, atomic current-slot switch, and exact-command resume/discard inspection. MEASURED GAP at HEAD 1ce0059: @moe/store has transaction/WAL integrity and runner artifact CAS has file fsync/rename precedent, but repo-wide searches find no RecoveryAnchor, inactive database slot, slot switch, restore installer, or anchor/database mismatch guard. NOT in scope: generating backup bytes, minting entropy/keys, external-effect inventory, R3 completion, ordinary restart, optimistic adoption, fault-suite evidence, or adding a second business authority. Hard dependencies: task-5606947a9d7d4f228dc63e6ce4dea69a (verified BackupGeneration) and task-684e6972c8c1418f8996ea3edd61f00c (fresh recovery identity binding). Owned paths: packages/store/src/recovery-anchor.* and focused @moe/store export wiring. Verification: pnpm --filter @moe/store typecheck && pnpm --filter @moe/store test.
definitionOfDone: The production installer persists one versioned OS-protected anchor record with active/inactive slots and `PREPARED|INSTALLED` state, bound to restore command, complete backup-generation digest, incarnation, and key epoch; the anchor is excluded from restored payload bytes.

Installation writes only the inactive slot, transactionally installs the fresh incarnation/key epoch, revokes all restored credentials/grants, records `QUIESCED/RECOVERY_REQUIRED`, persists database and reachable artifacts, read-back verifies them, then performs one atomic current-slot switch before marking the anchor `INSTALLED`.

Injected failure at prepare, inactive install, transaction, file fsync, directory persistence, verification, switch, or installed-marker boundary exposes either the prior active slot or one verified quiesced restored slot; never mixed slots or mutating authority.

Anchor/database/command/incarnation mismatch, absent persistence proof, or unverifiable inactive bytes refuses mutating open with distinct stable `RECOVERY_ANCHOR_*` code at layer `RECOVERY_ANCHOR`; allowed output is limited to exact install inspection/resume/discard.

Repeated resume of the same prepared command reuses its prepared identity, while a new command for the identical generation requires a different incarnation/key epoch; focused tests assert code/layer and mutation-check the production slot selector.

Failure tests assert exact stable code and `RECOVERY_ANCHOR` layer, and each declared injection point must be generated at least once.

SURFACE THE TESTS PIN, designed here so step 4 implements against a fixed contract rather than the reverse:
- `prepareRecoveryAnchor(request)` -> PREPARED record; `installRecoveryAnchor(request)` -> INSTALLED record; `selectInactiveSlot(slot)` -> the other slot.
- Record fields: anchorCodecVersion, state, currentSlot, targetSlot, restoreCommandId, generationDigest, incarnationRef, keyEpochRef, preparedAt, preparedIdentity, anchorDigest, plus the three taskRail-2 metadata fields restoredAuthorityRevoked / restoredLifecycle / restoredReadiness.

TWO DIGESTS, and the split is deliberate because one value cannot satisfy both DoD 1 and DoD 5. `preparedIdentity` is the FENCE — it binds command, generation, incarnation, key epoch and preparedAt, and must survive PREPARED -> INSTALLED unchanged so DoD 5's "repeated resume reuses its prepared identity" is expressible. `anchorDigest` covers the whole record INCLUDING state and currentSlot, so DoD 1's "perturbing any of them yields a different anchor identity" holds across the transition too. A test asserts both directions on one install: preparedIdentity equal, anchorDigest different.

DoD 1 FIELD SWEEP — the case list is HAND-WRITTEN (IDENTITY_BOUND_FIELDS, 5 entries) with two guards on the generator itself: a literal `.length).toBe(5)` and an exact name-set equality against the perturbation table's own keys. Deriving the sweep from Object.keys(anchor) would shrink silently with the record and still report every case as covered, which is the defect I want closed here rather than discovered in review.

DoD 1 EXCLUSION CLAUSE, with a positive control. After a real install the test walks EVERY file under <root>/slots recursively and asserts neither preparedIdentity nor anchorDigest appears in any of their bytes. The control reads the published anchor file first and asserts the identity IS findable there as bytes — otherwise "not found in the payload" could just mean the value is unsearchable and the assertion would pass against a broken search.

SLOT LITERALS: the tests import RECOVERY_BINDING_SLOTS and index it ([0]/[1]) rather than writing "ACTIVE"/"PENDING", so a slot rename in the install layer desynchronises loudly. `selectInactiveSlot` is exercised over every declared slot with an involution check (selectInactiveSlot(selectInactiveSlot(s)) === s), which is what makes step 6's selector mutation drill land on a named case.

implementationPlan.description:
TDD RED for the install ordering and the failure-injection matrix (DoD 2 and DoD 3) — the heart of this task.

DoD 2's ORDER is the property: write ONLY the inactive slot; transactionally install the fresh incarnation/key epoch; record the revocation and QUIESCED/RECOVERY_REQUIRED facts as anchor METADATA (taskRail 2); persist database and reachable artifacts; READ-BACK VERIFY them; then ONE atomic current-slot switch; and only then mark INSTALLED. Assert the sequence, not just the end state — a run that reaches INSTALLED by a different order has not proved crash safety.

DoD 3 requires injecting failure at EACH boundary: prepare, inactive install, transaction, file fsync, directory persistence, verification, switch, and installed-marker. For every one, assert the observable outcome is EITHER the prior active slot OR one verified quiesced restored slot — NEVER a mixed state and never mutating authority. Eight injections, eight assertions; a single shared "it failed cleanly" helper does not satisfy this.

The strongest form: after each injected failure, re-open the store fresh and assert which slot is current and that its bytes verify. Crash safety is a property of what a NEW reader sees, not of what the failing process returned.

Assert a generated sweep produced a NON-ZERO case count and that each declared injection point was actually generated — a sweep that silently produces zero cases passes while testing nothing.
implementationPlan.note:
TDD RED for DoD 2 + DoD 3. Appended 3 ordering cases and the 8-case injection matrix to recovery-anchor.test.ts (now 423 lines; local convention for this package runs 363-681, so one file is right). Still import-level RED, now on RECOVERY_ANCHOR_DATABASE_NAME: 1 failed | 36 passed (37) Test Files. Weak by construction until step 4 lands the modules — the load-bearing red is next.

ORDERING ASSERTED AS A SEQUENCE, not an end state. The `injectFault` seam is used two ways: given a NON-throwing observer it records every boundary the install crosses, and the test asserts the recorded array `toEqual([...RECOVERY_ANCHOR_FAULT_POINTS])` — exact order and exact length, so a boundary crossed twice, skipped, or reordered fails. A second case pins the eight names literally with a hand-written `.length).toBe(8)` and a Set-size dedup check, so the declared list cannot shrink and take the sweep with it.

THE MATRIX IS NOT EIGHT COPIES OF ONE ASSERTION, which the step explicitly forbids. Cases are generated from the production const but graded against a HAND-WRITTEN table, EXPECTED_AFTER_FAULT, mapping each boundary to PRIOR or RESTORED. Seven must leave the prior slot current; exactly ONE — INSTALLED_MARKER, the only boundary after the switch lands — may expose the newly restored slot. Two guards on the table itself: exact name-set equality against the fault-point const, and a literal assertion that exactly one entry is RESTORED. Reorder the switch against any other boundary and a row moves and reddens. That asymmetry is what makes the sweep non-vacuous.

FAULTS ARE THROWN, NOT RETURNED, deliberately. An injected fault propagates out of `installRecoveryAnchor` (`.rejects.toThrow`), because a crash is not a graceful refusal — letting production convert it into a tidy refusal would allow it to clean up after itself and the matrix would stop measuring crash safety. Every assertion is then made by a FRESH `inspectRecoveryAnchor(root)`, never from the return of the call that died.

"NEVER MIXED" IS MEASURED ON TWO INDEPENDENT AXES, because either alone is satisfiable by a half-written slot. `markersIn` reads every ARTIFACT in the current slot and requires the generation-marker set be exactly one value; `slotIncarnation` opens that slot's real database and requires the incarnation the transaction stamped to name the SAME generation. Mixed = gen2 artifacts beside a gen1-stamped database, and that now fails. `markersIn` additionally asserts it found exactly 2 artifacts — a slot that lost its payload would otherwise return an empty set, compare equal to nothing, and read as a pass.

DESIGN CORRECTION MADE WHILE WRITING, it changes the request contract so it is recorded rather than left in the diff: my first draft passed a marker string as `databaseBytes`. That cannot work — the installer opens what it writes and runs the LANDED `installRecoveryBinding` against it, so the payload must carry a genuine bootstrapped SQLite database. Tests mint one with `SqliteEventStore.openForProject(...).close()` and read the bytes. This also settles where the fresh incarnation goes: into the RESTORED database in the inactive slot, which is what makes the PRIOR/RESTORED distinction observable at all.

ONE PROPERTY THE PREPARE BOUNDARY FORCED. Preparing a second restore must not overwrite the pointer to the live slot, or a crash just after prepare orphans a good slot. The record therefore carries currentSlot AND targetSlot together, so a new PREPARED anchor keeps naming the live slot as current while naming its own target. The matrix asserts it: after a fault at PREPARE the fresh reader still lands on gen1, verified.

Per DoD 3's "never mutating authority", every post-fault inspection also pins `mutatingOpenAllowed === false`, `allowedOperations` sorted equal to ["DISCARD","INSPECT","RESUME"], and `restoredReadiness === "RECOVERY_REQUIRED"`.

THE ONE RED THAT MATTERED, and production was wrong, not the test. First full run: 27/28, failing on "exposes one whole verified slot when the install dies at PREPARE" with `expected true to be false` at the `mutatingOpenAllowed` assertion. Cause: I had written `mutatingOpenAllowed = slotVerified && state === "INSTALLED"`, and a crash at PREPARE leaves the PRIOR completed anchor in place — verified and INSTALLED — so the anchor granted a mutating open. That is exactly the authority taskRail 2 says this module does not have. INSTALLED means the anchor SELECTED a database, not that recovery finished; every record permanently carries restoredReadiness RECOVERY_REQUIRED and only the reducer may clear it. Fixed in production: `mutatingOpenAllowed` is now the literal type `false`.

An always-false boolean is a weak assertion, so I did not leave it as the only signal. Added `mutatingOpenRefusal`, which VARIES: the specific verification fault (PERSISTENCE_UNPROVEN / SLOT_UNVERIFIABLE / DATABASE_MISMATCH) when the current slot fails, otherwise the new RECOVERY_ANCHOR_RECOVERY_REQUIRED. That is DoD 4's "distinct stable code" and it is drillable.

DESIGN CHANGE THE MATRIX FORCED — worth recording because it is not obvious. Verification cannot be judged against the anchor. After a crash the fresh reader usually has to verify the slot the install was NOT writing, and grading gen1's slot against the in-flight gen2 anchor's digests fails a slot that is perfectly intact. So each slot carries its OWN `slot-manifest.json` persistence proof and is verified against that. The manifest deliberately holds no anchor identity, so DoD 1's exclusion assertion still passes over it.

The database is verified SEMANTICALLY rather than by byte digest, because the install transaction rewrites the file after it is written: verification reopens the slot database and requires the stamped binding's incarnationRef and keyEpochRef to match the slot manifest. That proves the transaction committed durably, which a byte comparison against the pre-transaction bytes could not.

implementationPlan.description:
DoD 5 — resume and re-prepare identity, which is subtler than it reads. Repeated resume of the SAME prepared command must reuse its prepared identity (idempotent, no second anchor, same receipt). But a NEW command for the IDENTICAL backup generation must REQUIRE a different incarnation and key epoch — otherwise a replayed restore could reuse a fence that the first attempt already consumed.

Test both directions explicitly, and test the refusal: a new command presenting the SAME incarnation/key epoch for the same generation refuses with an exact anchor code. RECOVERY_INSTALL_INCARNATION_CONFLICT already exists in the install vocabulary — check whether it is the right code before minting an anchor-level one.

This is the clause that makes the anchor a fence rather than a cache, so assert the identity reuse by exact equality and the required-difference by exact inequality.
implementationPlan.note:
DoD 5 done, and it turned up a real production bug that my own first set of passing tests did not catch. Gate: typecheck 0, test 0, 37 files / 423 tests (was 412 after step 4).

THE BUG, found by asking what the test would still pass with. "resumes repeatedly without minting a new identity" went green on the first run — it only compared preparedIdentity. But after the switch `currentSlot === targetSlot`, so re-entering the protocol on a settled install writes the restored payload into the slot that is now LIVE. That is precisely the one thing this module exists never to do, and my resume path did it while every assertion stayed green.

Fixed in production with `settledInstall`: an install whose stored anchor is INSTALLED and whose preparedIdentity matches returns that record verbatim without re-running. Completion is idempotent on the fence.

THE TEST THAT CATCHES IT, because markers cannot. A re-run writes the SAME bytes back, so comparing generation markers or digests before and after sees nothing. The new case "never re-enters the protocol against an install that already completed" writes a sentinel file into the live slot between install and resume and asserts it survives — the sentinel only disappears if the slot was cleared. That distinguishes "left alone" from "rebuilt identically", which no content comparison can.

DRILLED IT RATHER THAN ASSERTING IT. Removed the two-line settled-install guard (anchor count checked == 1 before editing, aborts otherwise) and re-ran: `1 failed | 422 passed (423)`, the single failure being `× never re-enters the protocol against an install that already completed`. Exactly the named test, nothing else — so the guard is load-bearing and the test is what pins it. Restored by reverse-replace, and since the file is UNTRACKED `git diff` is blind, so I verified by hash instead: baseline 91bd094ea24d25d9af2ed4789622129cff87d375, mutated 31711118acbb5c3fa31565a477f175fd80e96309, restored back to 91bd094e — byte-exact. Suite green again at 423.

WHY I MINTED AN ANCHOR CODE INSTEAD OF REUSING RECOVERY_INSTALL_INCARNATION_CONFLICT, which the step told me to check first. The install code sits at layer RECOVERY_INSTALL_TRANSACTION and models a SQLite UNIQUE violation on incarnation_ref inside one database — it can only fire once a database has been opened and written. The anchor fault is a different thing: a fence reused ACROSS restore commands, detected before any database is touched. Reusing that code would assert a database constraint fired when none did, and would make DoD 4's layer assertion unpinnable. So RECOVERY_ANCHOR_INCARNATION_REUSED at layer RECOVERY_ANCHOR, and the test asserts `RECOVERY_INSTALL_REASON_CODES` does NOT contain it — the two vocabularies are provably disjoint at that point.

THE FENCE IS TESTED IN THREE LEGS, not one, because a guard checking only the incarnation would pass a single-leg test: reusing both halves, the incarnation alone, and the key epoch alone are separate named cases, all requiring RECOVERY_ANCHOR_INCARNATION_REUSED. The positive direction is asserted by exact INEQUALITY (a new command with both halves fresh gets a different preparedIdentity on the same generationDigest), and reuse by exact EQUALITY (re-preparing the same command returns the same identity AND leaves exactly one anchor file on disk — a fence that can be minted twice is a cache).

I ALSO IMPLEMENTED THE OPERATIONS I HAD ALREADY DECLARED. `allowedOperations` named INSPECT/RESUME/DISCARD while only inspect existed, which is exactly the kind of claim that detaches from its subject. `resumeRecoveryAnchor` refuses RECOVERY_ANCHOR_COMMAND_MISMATCH if the stored anchor belongs to another command, so a replayed restore cannot ride another attempt's preparation. `discardRecoveryAnchor` derives its target from `currentSlot` via selectInactiveSlot rather than from `targetSlot` — after a completed install those are equal, and using targetSlot would delete the live slot.

Publish from the store root and mutation-drill. Add a curated named block to packages/store/src/index.ts in its existing explicit style (the prerequisite's block sits at :66-80 — match it, append, do not reorder neighbours; the barrel is shared state).

(a) Write the ACTIVE slot before the switch — a DoD 3 injection case must redden, proving the write-inactive-only discipline is what provides crash safety. (b) Mark INSTALLED before the read-back verification — the verification-boundary case must redden. (c) Perform the slot switch non-atomically — a fresh-reader assertion must redden. (d) Let a resume mint a new prepared identity — the DoD 5 reuse case must redden. (e) Accept the same incarnation for a new command on the same generation — the conflict refusal must redden. (f) Change only the refusing LAYER on one anchor refusal — a layer assertion must redden independently of the code.
